items.title: 67460_Sammy Price oral history interview
items.q: we'd go to Mary Lou William's

ctx.x: going down to a company...the same company that Guy Lombardo was, you know what I mean, the King...and Bing Crosby...the first check I ever saw for a million dollars, you know what I mean, Bing had it, and all that. Can you imagine Sammy Price...again, I go back to that man with the trumpet, and that woman and Ella B. Moore, and then Kansas City with Ellis Burden and all the way up the line. Can you imagine my being in New York City in 1937 or early '38 making a hundred dollars for a day's work! Three hours!

Then I had an opportunity...this is my day, this would be my schedule. I'd have a recording date at 9 o'clock. From 9 to 12. I'd go back home, eat breakfast, go back to bed. Wake up at 6. Come out to Mrs. Frazier's restaurant where a lot of people used to eat 'cause there were not that many places to eat. You couldn't eat in Frank's in those days, or you could, but you knew you'd have to be with some white person, all right? Go to Mrs. Frazier's and eat, after I go to Mrs. Frazier's and eat, 6 o'clock, may go…
*Mary Lou's husband at the time, John Williams, saxophonist with the Andy Kirk orchestra.

items.title: 53571_Mary Lou Williams oral history interview
items.q: Sammy Price happened to be playing in the club one night

ctx.x: They put them in the music scene because they followed all the musicians. They were crazy about musicians but they were two beautiful girls and I think their father was a big political leader and a wonderful Italian man off of Fifth Avenue. Fifth Avenue was a pretty rough street; after jam sessions certain nights we'd all go there. Lucille and Louise were not allowed out, not unless their mother asked me if I was going along with them. I don't know why she thought I could protect them. They were both older than…
